newsitem.title: JAPAN: TIFFE FIRMER BUT RISES BLOCKED DESPITE STOCK FALL.
newsitem.headline: TIFFE FIRMER BUT RISES BLOCKED DESPITE STOCK FALL.

text.p: The benchmark three-month March euroyen futures contract settled firmer but off earlier highs in Tokyo on Monday, despite heavy losses in Tokyo stocks that saw the Nikkei fall four percent.

The key Nikkei-225 index ended down 780.28, at 18,824.18. But euroyen traders said that many in the market wanted to see if this were merely temporary or the start of a trend, and thus refrained from buying.

"There was a feeling in the market that the reasons for the Nikkei fall were not that closely linked to Japan, and this is keeping many from buying until they verify whether a trend is beginning or not," one trust bank trader said.
The Nikkei's fall was attributed primarily to a stronger yen and Friday's sharp fall in U.S. stocks.
The key March contract settled at 99.22, up 0.01, after rising as far as 99.24 in early trade. It briefly touched a low of 99.21. Turnover was a thin 23,468 contracts.
Traders said additional wariness came from the fact that key March is hovering close to its contract high.
"Until the market has confirmation that today's moves were not a fluke, few are willing to trade the contract much higher, given a sense that it is quite strong already," a city bank trader said.
But with little in the way of selling factors seen over the short-term, the downside will remain solid. Some traders said they expected support to hold near 99.20, partly for technical reasons.
Japanese government bonds (JGBs) also failed to rise on the Nikkei fall, primarily because many investors appeared to be out of the market due to summer holidays.
Overnight call money was being traded mostly at 0.47 percent, and traders said the weighted average was likely to be 0.47 percent as well, up from 0.46 percent on Friday.
As the market had expected, the Bank of Japan (BOJ) refrained from performing its usual 0020 GMT money market operation, leaving the market in a neutral condition.
Around 20 billion yen worth of three-month certificates of deposit (CDs) were issued at 0.58 percent, the lowest since May 23 and down from 0.59 percent on Friday.
No two-month or one-month CDs had been issued as of 0700 GMT.
